COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Scaling Reasoning Hop Exposes Weaknesses: Demystifying and Improving Hop Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates where errors occur in reasoning hop generalization (RQ1) and why these errors arise (RQ2), focusing on the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Test-time Correction of Reasoning (TCR), a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates erroneous processing heads to improve reasoning hop generalization, based on mechanistic insights into internal competition mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCR effectively improves reasoning hop generalization by dynamically deactivating erroneous processing heads, demonstrating the potential of test-time interventions based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Errors in reasoning hop generalization are dominated by token-level erroneous predictions of a few specific error types, enabling focused diagnosis.
These token-level errors stem from an internal competition mechanism: correct trajectories coexist with erroneous ones but are actively suppressed by erroneous processing heads; knocking out such heads can restore correct predictions.
The proposed TCR method, which automatically and dynamically deactivates erroneous processing heads, consistently improves reasoning hop generalization across tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become the standard paradigm for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex problems. However, recent studies reveal a sharp performance drop in reasoning hop generalization scenarios, where the required number of reasoning steps exceeds training distributions while the underlying algorithm remains unchanged. The internal mechanisms driving this failure remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on tasks from multiple domains, and find that errors concentrate at token positions of a few critical error types, rather than being uniformly distributed. Closer inspection reveals that these token-level erroneous predictions stem from internal competition mechanisms: certain attention heads, termed erroneous processing heads (ep heads), tip the balance by amplifying incorrect reasoning trajectories while suppressing correct ones. Notably, removing individual ep heads during inference can often restore the correct predictions. Motivated by these insights, we propose test-time correction of reasoning, a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates ep heads in the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across different tasks and LLMs show that it consistently improves reasoning hop generalization, highlighting both its effectiveness and potential.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: Does Huginn exhibit signs of latent chain-of-thought reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: We find limited evidence of interpretable latent chain-of-thought reasoning in the depth-recurrent transformer Huginn-3.5B, and uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks.
papers.conclusion: We find little evidence of structured latent chain-of-thought reasoning in Huginn, but it may be more subtle or distributed than our tools can detect.
papers.key_findings:
Probing inconsistencies across blocks in Huginn's depth-recurrent architecture: hidden state interpretability depends heavily on block index and decoding method.
Token rank trajectory analysis provides little evidence for latent CoT reasoning.
Scaling recurrence depth fails to match explicit reasoning: increasing recurrent steps only marginally improves performance and falls short of explicit CoT prompting.
papers.limitation: The results do not definitively rule out the presence of latent CoT; it may be more subtle or distributed than our employed tools can detect.
future_direction: Apply more advanced probing techniques, such as activation patching, to uncover finer-grained reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has enabled transformer-based language models to excel at complex mathematics and multi-step planning. However, in standard decoder-only architectures, these reasoning steps are externalized in natural language, improving interpretability at the cost of efficiency. To capture reasoning that is not easily represented in words, many works have explored recurrent architectures that aim to internalize reasoning in latent space, potentially supporting latent CoT. In this paper, we investigate whether such reasoning structures emerge in Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer that reuses layers at inference time without increasing parameter count. We examine the model's internal behavior on arithmetic tasks using a suite of probing techniques including the Logit Lens and Coda Lens. Our findings reveal limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT by tracking rank trajectories of final and intermediate result tokens. Furthermore, we uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks, where the interpretability of hidden states depends heavily on both the layer index and the decoding method. Finally, we empirically show that increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal gains and falls well short of models that explicitly externalize reasoning steps. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/huginn-latent-cot.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models perform multi-step reasoning? The paper aims to uncover the reasoning mechanisms (thought processes) used by language models in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF), which combines circuit analysis and self-influence functions to trace and analyze the reasoning pathways of language models, demonstrating its application on GPT-2 for the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that SICAF successfully maps reasoning pathways in language models, revealing a hierarchical reasoning structure similar to human thought processes.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace the thought process of language models during complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified by EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL are more faithful and compact than those identified by EAP.
The model's key parameters are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The reasoning process follows a hierarchical structure: early layers identify entities, middle layers interpret actions, and final layers synthesize information.
Self-influence scores show how token importance changes across layers, revealing the reasoning path.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
Our work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of this approach across varied tasks and model architectures
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success; however, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque due to the complexity of non-linear interactions and high-dimensional operations. While previous studies have demonstrated that these models implicitly embed reasoning trees, humans typically employ various distinct logical reasoning mechanisms to complete the same task. It is still unclear which multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve such tasks. In this paper, we aim to address this question by investigating the mechanistic interpretability of language models, particularly in the context of multi-step reasoning tasks. Specifically, we employ circuit analysis and self-influence functions to evaluate the changing importance of each token throughout the reasoning process, allowing us to map the reasoning paths adopted by the model. We apply this methodology to the GPT-2 model on a prediction task (IOI) and demonstrate that the underlying circuits reveal a human-interpretable reasoning process used by the model.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the representational capacity of neural language models (LMs) when augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning? Specifically, can CoT-augmented LMs represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in a probabilistic setting and shows that recurrent and transformer language models augmented with CoT reasoning can represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning increases the computational power of neural language models by allowing them to perform additional sequential computation and keep track of execution trajectories, effectively introducing non-determinism and enabling simulation of probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.key_findings:
CoT-augmented constant-precision RNN LMs are equivalent to probabilistic finite-state automata (PFSAs), whereas without CoT they are equivalent to deterministic PFSAs.
CoT-augmented RNN LMs with linearly bounded precision and transformer LMs with logarithmically bounded precision can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine.
CoT reasoning provides a principled way to overcome the limitation of deterministic computation in fixed-precision neural models, allowing them to simulate non-deterministic automata.

papers.title: Who Reasons in the Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention is primarily responsible for reasoning capabilities in LLMs, and introduces Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools to probe and analyze internal behaviors, providing evidence for this hypothesis.
papers.conclusion: The work hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) module plays a central role in enabling reasoning capabilities in LLMs. The proposed Stethoscope for Networks (SfN) provides diagnostic tools that offer evidence for this hypothesis and open new directions for efficient and modular LLM training.
papers.key_findings:
The o_proj module exhibits the largest or second-largest weight changes during reasoning fine-tuning across model sizes (Delta Stethoscope).
Merging only the o_proj modules from a reasoning model into a base model can improve reasoning ability without further tuning (Merge Stethoscope).
Fine-tuning only o_proj (and layernorm, embed_tokens, lm_head) can achieve strong reasoning performance, with faster training and lower memory usage compared to full fine-tuning (Freeze Stethoscope).
Destroying o_proj does not harm conversational ability, while destroying MLP components or q/k_proj severely degrades it, suggesting a division of labor (Destruction Stethoscope).
The findings suggest o_proj is crucial for reasoning, while other modules primarily support conversational fluency.
papers.limitation:
Findings are primarily based on a limited set of model families and reasoning benchmarks, and may not generalize to all architectures or tasks.
Some diagnostic results rely on qualitative assessments rather than statistical validation.
A theoretical understanding of o_proj's function in reasoning remains to be established.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), the process of endowing them with new capabilities--such as mathematical reasoning--remains largely empirical and opaque. A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting. In this work, we hypothesize that the reasoning capabilities in well-trained LLMs are primarily attributed to the output projection module (oproj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention (MHSA) mechanism. To support this hypothesis, we introduce Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools designed to probe and analyze the internal behaviors of LLMs. Using SfN, we provide both circumstantial and empirical evidence suggesting that oproj plays a central role in enabling reasoning, whereas other modules contribute more to fluent dialogue. These findings offer a new perspective on LLM interpretability and open avenues for more targeted training strategies, potentially enabling more efficient and specialized LLMs.

papers.title: Diversity of Transformer Layers: One Aspect of Parameter Scaling Laws
papers.research_question: How do the internal layer dynamics (specifically the diversity of layer outputs) in Transformers relate to parameter scaling laws?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diversity of predictions from each module in the Transformer residual stream is crucial for performance, and that adding layers improves performance only when layers are diverse, with diminishing returns that align with parameter scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: The diversity of predictions from each module on the residual stream is important for improving Transformer performance, and the effectiveness of adding layers diminishes as the number of layers increases, consistent with parameter scaling laws.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse.
Diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth.
Adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently (are diverse).
The performance gains from increasing layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by parameter scaling laws.
Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm these theoretical properties.
papers.limitation: The decomposition based on mean squared error (MSE) is specific to logits, and there may be a gap when targeting tasks that use softmax to obtain probability, such as uncertainty estimation, confidence calibration, and beam decoding. Furthermore, using information-theoretic diversity for actual tasks requires calculating the probability density of the representation on the residual stream, which is difficult without approximation or assumptions.
papers.abstract: Transformers deliver outstanding performance across a wide range of tasks and are now a dominant backbone architecture for large language models (LLMs). Their task-solving performance is improved by increasing parameter size, as shown in the recent studies on parameter scaling laws. Although recent mechanistic-interpretability studies have deepened our understanding of the internal behavior of Transformers by analyzing their residual stream, the relationship between these internal mechanisms and the parameter scaling laws remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we focus on layers and their size, which mainly decide the parameter size of Transformers. For this purpose, we first theoretically investigate the layers within the residual stream through a bias-diversity decomposition. The decomposition separates (i) bias, the error of each layer's output from the ground truth, and (ii) diversity, which indicates how much the outputs of each layer differ from each other. Analyzing Transformers under this theory reveals that performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse. We show that diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth. Finally, we introduce an information-theoretic diversity and show our main findings that adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently, i.e., are diverse. We also reveal the performance gains from increasing the number of layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by the parameter scaling laws. Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm the theoretical properties derived in this study.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Use Their Depth?
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally structure their computations during inference and use their depth layer-by-layer to arrive at predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a 'Guess-then-Refine' framework showing that LLMs use early layers for statistical guesses (high-frequency tokens) and later layers for contextual refinement, with depth usage varying by task complexity.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are early statistical guessers and late contextual integrators, using depth flexibly based on task complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Early LLM layers propose high-frequency tokens as statistical guesses due to lack of contextual information.
Early layer guesses are heavily refined in later layers, with 80% of early top-ranked guesses replaced.
In multiple-choice tasks, early layers collect valid options and later layers reason between them.
In multi-token fact recall, the first token requires more computational depth than subsequent tokens.
Function words (e.g., determiners, prepositions) are predicted correctly earlier than content words (nouns, verbs).
papers.limitation: Analysis limited to next-token prediction, fact recall, and downstream tasks; does not cover reasoning or chain-of-thought tasks.
future_direction: Analysis for reasoning and chain-of-thought tasks
Analysis of more recent reasoning models
papers.abstract: Growing evidence suggests that large language models do not use their depth uniformly, yet we still lack a fine-grained understanding of their layer-wise prediction dynamics. In this paper, we trace the intermediate representations of several open-weight models during inference and reveal a structured and nuanced use of depth. Specifically, we propose a "Guess-then-Refine" framework that explains how LLMs internally structure their computations to make predictions. We first show that the top-ranked predictions in early LLM layers are composed primarily of high-frequency tokens, which act as statistical guesses proposed by the model early on due to the lack of appropriate contextual information. As contextual information develops deeper into the model, these initial guesses get refined into contextually appropriate tokens. Even high-frequency token predictions from early layers get refined >70% of the time, indicating that correct token prediction is not "one-and-done". We then go beyond frequency-based prediction to examine the dynamic usage of layer depth across three case studies. (i) Part-of-speech analysis shows that function words are, on average, the earliest to be predicted correctly. (ii) Fact recall task analysis shows that, in a multi-token answer, the first token requires more computational depth than the rest. (iii) Multiple-choice task analysis shows that the model identifies the format of the response within the first half of the layers, but finalizes its response only toward the end. Together, our results provide a detailed view of depth usage in LLMs, shedding light on the layer-by-layer computations that underlie successful predictions and providing insights for future works to improve computational efficiency in transformer-based models.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization? The paper investigates the connection between cross-lingual generalization and compression during pre-training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared, cross-lingual abstractions, observable in the alignment of concept-specific neurons.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models is driven by compression during pre-training, leading to shared neural representations for concepts across languages, independent of the original language encoding.
papers.key_findings:
During pre-training, model representations evolve from language-specific to cross-lingual abstractions, consistent with a compression effect.
Language identification probing shows a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons become increasingly aligned across languages for the same semantic concepts as training progresses.
Manipulating concept-specific neurons identified in one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language, demonstrating shared neural representations.
papers.limitation:
The number of available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited.
The concept dataset is created by machine translation, which may introduce noise and errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision. We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses. Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions. For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts. By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages. Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.

papers.title: First Heuristic Then Rational: Dynamic Use of Heuristics in Language Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: Do language models use a systematic strategy similar to humans when solving complex tasks, specifically by relying on heuristics more in earlier reasoning stages and becoming more rational as they approach the answer?
papers.core_contribution: Language models dynamically transition from heuristic to rational reasoning during multi-step problem-solving, relying more on heuristics when the answer is distant and less as they get closer, indicating a limited capacity to backtrack future steps.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers a systematic strategy in LMs' multi-step reasoning: a dynamic transition from heuristic to rational reasoning as they progress step-by-step toward an answer.
papers.key_findings:
LMs rely more heavily on heuristics (e.g., lexical overlap) in earlier reasoning steps where the goal is distant.
Reliance on heuristics decreases as LMs progress closer to the final answer through reasoning steps.
Different models exhibit varying preferences for heuristic types (e.g., lexical overlap vs. position).
LMs have a limited capacity to track future reasoning paths, leading to heuristic use when many steps remain.
The dynamic strategy is somewhat human-like, employing heuristics first before switching to rational reasoning.
papers.limitation:
The study focused only on four specific language models and two arithmetic tasks.
Findings are based solely on model outputs (behavioral analysis), not internal mechanisms.
future_direction: Increasing the coverage of models and tasks to generalize findings.
Constructing controlled but natural datasets to evaluate reasoning strategies.
Elucidating the underlying mechanisms inside the model and the source of these biases.
papers.abstract: Multi-step reasoning instruction, such as chain-of-thought prompting, is widely adopted to explore better language models (LMs) performance. We report on the systematic strategy that LMs employ in such a multi-step reasoning process. Our controlled experiments reveal that LMs rely more heavily on heuristics, such as lexical overlap, in the earlier stages of reasoning, where more reasoning steps remain to reach a goal. Conversely, their reliance on heuristics decreases as LMs progress closer to the final answer through multiple reasoning steps. This suggests that LMs can backtrack only a limited number of future steps and dynamically combine heuristic strategies with rationale ones in tasks involving multi-step reasoning.

papers.title: Language Models Implement Simple Word2Vec-style Vector Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How do language models solve relational tasks in in-context learning? Do they use a simple vector arithmetic mechanism similar to Word2Vec?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models implement a simple vector arithmetic mechanism via FFN updates to solve relational tasks in-context, and this mechanism is specific to tasks requiring retrieval from pretraining memory.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LMs sometimes use simple vector arithmetic mechanisms for relational tasks, offering optimism for interpretability and potential for intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LMs exhibit argument-function processing: they first represent the argument in the residual stream and then apply a function via an FFN update.
The function application is implemented by mid-to-late layer FFNs and is modular (can be transferred to new contexts).
This mechanism is specific to abstractive tasks (requiring retrieval from pretraining memory) and not used in extractive tasks.
The mechanism is similar to Word2Vec-style vector arithmetic and works only for one-to-one relations.
The processing signature becomes sharper with larger models.
papers.limitation:
The intervention is not perfect; errors occur for less frequent associations and due to tokenization.
The mechanism only applies to one-to-one relations, similar to static embeddings.
The intervention procedure may not generalize perfectly across models (e.g., weaker effects on GPT-J).
future_direction: Generalize the findings to model-agnostic phenomena.
Understand how and when different mechanisms for factual recall interact.
Use processing signatures for runtime evaluation and intervention to prevent unwanted behavior.
papers.abstract: Jack Merullo, Carsten Eickhoff, Ellie Pavlick. Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
papers.research_question: What is the underlying structure of language model capabilities? Can they be explained by a small number of latent factors, and how do these factors relate to model properties like size and instruction tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three latent factors (reasoning, comprehension, and core language modeling) that explain much of the variance in LLM performance across diverse tasks, and shows that these abilities have distinct relationships with model size and instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a first step towards a theoretical understanding of LLM capabilities, demonstrating a consistent underlying structure and offering a basis for more efficient benchmarking and prediction of model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Three latent factors (reasoning, comprehension, and core language modeling) explain a high proportion of variance in LLM performance across 27 cognitive tasks.
Model size is positively correlated with all three factors, but the correlation is strongest for comprehension.
Instruction tuning is negatively correlated with language modeling ability but positively correlated with reasoning ability.
The three factors are moderately correlated with each other, similar to patterns observed in human cognitive abilities.
The factor structure suggests benchmarks could be streamlined by focusing on tasks that tap into each broad ability, enabling more efficient evaluation.
papers.limitation:
The relatively small sample of LLMs (29 models) limits generalizability and requires replication with larger samples.
The interpretation of factors in factor analysis is inherently somewhat subjective, and some tasks did not load neatly on the expected factors.
Many HELM tasks were designed based on format rather than cognitive demands, making clean separation of capabilities difficult.
future_direction: Replicate the findings with a larger sample of language models.
Confirm the validity of the factor interpretations through further investigation.
Include tasks specifically designed to test particular cognitive abilities in future benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Building a theoretical understanding of the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is vital for our ability to predict and explain the behavior of these systems. Here, we investigate the structure of LLM capabilities by extracting latent capabilities from patterns of individual differences across a varied population of LLMs. Using a combination of Bayesian and frequentist factor analysis, we analyzed data from 29 different LLMs across 27 cognitive tasks. We found evidence that LLM capabilities are not monolithic. Instead, they are better explained by three well-delineated factors that represent reasoning, comprehension and core language modeling. Moreover, we found that these three factors can explain a high proportion of the variance in model performance. These results reveal a consistent structure in the capabilities of different LLMs and demonstrate the multifaceted nature of these capabilities. We also found that the three abilities show different relationships to model properties such as model size and instruction tuning. These patterns help refine our understanding of scaling laws and indicate that changes to a model that improve one ability might simultaneously impair others. Based on these findings, we suggest that benchmarks could be streamlined by focusing on tasks that tap into each broad model ability.

papers.title: ConTrans: Weak-to-Strong Alignment Engineering via Concept Transplantation
papers.research_question: Can weak-to-strong alignment supervision be achieved internally within the latent feature space of LLMs via concept transplantation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CONTRANS, a training-free framework for weak-to-strong alignment by refining concept vectors from a source LLM, reformulating them via affine transformation, and transplanting them into the residual stream of a target LLM.
papers.conclusion: CONTRANS provides an effective, internal, and training-free alternative for weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control via concept transplantation in the latent feature space.
papers.key_findings:
CONTRANS successfully transplants alignment concepts (e.g., truthfulness, toxicity) from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across different model families.
CONTRANS can surpass the truthfulness of instruction-tuned models on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
Concepts are formed during the pre-training phase and activated during the alignment phase.
Concept transplantation effectiveness depends on the similarity in base model architecture and pre-training data volume between source and target models.
The method requires only a few hundred positive/negative examples and incurs minimal inference overhead.
papers.limitation: CONTRANS is primarily designed for the implantation of a single concept and is not optimized for the fusion of multiple concepts.
papers.abstract: Ensuring large language models (LLM) behave consistently with human goals, values, and intentions is crucial for their safety but yet computationally expensive. To reduce the computational cost of alignment training of LLMs, especially for those with a huge number of parameters, and to reutilize learned value alignment, we propose ConTrans, a novel framework that enables weak-to-strong alignment transfer via concept transplantation. From the perspective of representation engineering, ConTrans refines concept vectors in value alignment from a source LLM (usually a weak yet aligned LLM). The refined concept vectors are then reformulated to adapt to the target LLM (usually a strong yet unaligned base LLM) via affine transformation. In the third step, ConTrans transplants the reformulated concept vectors into the residual stream of the target LLM. Experiments demonstrate the successful transplantation of a wide range of aligned concepts from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across multiple LLMs and LLM families. Remarkably, ConTrans even surpasses instruction-tuned models in terms of truthfulness. Experiment results validate the effectiveness of both inter-LLM-family and intra-LLM-family concept transplantation. Our work successfully demonstrates an alternative way to achieve weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature? Are simple probing techniques sufficient to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across diverse contexts such as logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be effectively identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize well to logical transformations, question answering, and contextual truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: Consistent truth directions emerge only in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize across logical transformations, QA, and contextual settings, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; stronger models show more consistent representations, especially across logical negation.
Simple linear probes (e.g., SVM, logistic regression) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist in the model.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic factual statements generalize to logical transformations (negation, conjunction, disjunction).
Truthfulness probes generalize to question answering tasks, including zero-shot, few-shot, and in-context learning settings, and are robust to false in-context examples.
Truthfulness probes can be applied to selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving the reliability of LLM outputs.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be what the probes actually measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truth.
Generalization analysis is limited to short-form QA; extending to long-form QA or instruction-following tasks may yield new insights.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; it is not established whether LLMs utilize the implicit truthfulness classification for predictions.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided Thought Space Exploration Leveraging LLM Intrinsic Reasoning
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities represented within LLMs’ internal activations, and how can these intrinsic abilities be effectively harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, a classifier-guided search framework that leverages linear separability of thoughtfulness in LLM activations to improve reasoning performance without human intervention.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe effectively leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through classifier-guided exploration, advancing understanding and enabling practical application without human intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Thoughtfulness is linearly separable in LLMs' activation space, with a simple linear classifier achieving over 80% performance.
Different LLMs encode thoughtfulness differently across representation types and layers.
The classifier's logit consistently assigns higher scores to correct, thoughtful responses regardless of length.
The ThoughtProbe framework outperforms baselines on multiple math reasoning benchmarks.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms single-branch selection and majority voting.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for segmenting intermediate thoughts may disrupt natural reasoning.
The gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Misalignment between training objectives (final outcomes) and guidance criteria (intermediate progress) may limit effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for tree node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Explore step-wise feedback or hierarchical evaluation to better align classifier training.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated to possess intrinsic reasoning capabilities that can emerge naturally when expanding the response space. However, the neural representation mechanisms underlying these intrinsic capabilities and approaches for their optimal utilization remain inadequately understood. In this work, we make the key discovery that a simple linear classifier can effectively detect intrinsic reasoning capabilities in LLMs' activation space, particularly within specific representation types and network layers. Based on this finding, we propose a classifier-guided search framework that strategically explore a tree-structured response space. In each node expansion, the classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by identifying and prioritizing more thoughtful reasoning directions for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We propose a branch-aggregation selection method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their thoughtfulness scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
